items.sloFit: the printed outcome targets the operating principle (Knowledge), while the comprehensive source prompt 'explain the working' ordinarily demands a connected mechanism and energy balance
items.scienceReview: The source's standard cyclic heat-engine model has a hot reservoir at T_H, a colder reservoir at T_C, and a working substance. During a complete cycle the engine absorbs heat Q_H, performs net work W_by and rejects heat Q_C with Q_H=W_by+Q_C for positive heat magnitudes. The cyclic working fluid has ΔU_cycle=0. Thermal efficiency is W_by/Q_H. Distinguish the idealized reservoir schematic from actual petrol engines, which are open systems and require careful cycle/energy accounting.
items.amendment: compulsory cycle/work/heat magnitude and engine-model qualification in any future teacher answer
items.reason: Original textbook pp.140–141 explains Figure 8.14 and writes W=Q1−Q2. A teacher answer must label heat input and heat rejected as positive magnitudes and must not treat W as the net result for any arbitrary noncyclic step, where ΔU may be nonzero. The source's 'every heat engine must have three parts' is a useful idealised schematic; a modern open-system internal-combustion engine should not be represented as literally identical to a closed working-fluid Carnot loop. The claimed historical priority of Carnot as 'first heat engine' is outside the requested physics mechanism and should not be repeated as independently verified history.

items.sloFit: direct printed outcome on the second law, including the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius formulations and physical interpretation
items.scienceReview: The Kelvin–Planck statement rules out a cyclic engine whose sole result is to absorb heat from one reservoir and convert all of it into net work. The Clausius statement rules out a cyclic device whose sole effect is to transfer heat from a colder body to a hotter body without any compensating effect (such as work input). Refrigerators move heat from cold to hot by using work. These statements concern the directional/possibility limits imposed by the Second Law; the First Law alone enforces energy conservation and is insufficient to enforce those limits.
items.amendment: compulsory sole-effect/cyclic qualification and equivalence-aware explanation before teacher marking
items.reason: The original source printed p.142 labels the statements as Lord Kelvin and Rudolf Clausius and phrases the first as single-reservoir heat fully converted to work while 'no change' remains in the working system. Without the essential cyclic-and-sole-result condition, students may wrongly conclude that no heat can ever be converted completely into work during a finite noncyclic transformation. Clausius likewise does not prohibit refrigerated cold-to-hot transfer when external work supplies a compensating effect. Preserve the publisher question and distinguish these as equivalent formulations of one Second Law rather than two independent principles.

items.sloFit: direct working-principle outcome, while explaining/deriving the efficiency relationship may demand more than the printed Knowledge-level efficiency-limit outcome
items.scienceReview: The original Carnot-cycle model is reversible and runs between two absolute reservoir temperatures T_H>T_C>0, on a closed ideal-gas working substance. In source Figures 8.16–8.17, its four reversible legs are (1) isothermal expansion absorbing Q_H at T_H, (2) adiabatic expansion from T_H to T_C, (3) isothermal compression rejecting Q_C at T_C, (4) adiabatic compression back to T_H. For one complete cycle ΔU_cycle=0, so W_net=Q_H−Q_C and η=W_net/Q_H=1−Q_C/Q_H. Only for a reversible Carnot cycle is Q_C/Q_H=T_C/T_H, yielding η_C=1−T_C/T_H with kelvin temperatures. W_net is the oriented enclosed area on the P–V diagram. Carnot's theorem makes η_C the reversible upper bound for engines between those reservoirs; real engines are generally less efficient.
items.amendment: compulsory reversible-ratio derivation, all four step/diagram continuity and Kelvin/model qualification; teacher review of observed cognitive demand
items.reason: Original pp.143–145 give the four steps, original Figures 8.16 and 8.17, Eq. 8.8 for net cycle work and Eq. 8.9 for Carnot efficiency. The source says broadly 'heat Q is proportional to absolute temperature T' before substituting the temperature ratio; this must be read specifically as a ratio for the reversible heat exchanges of the Carnot cycle, not as universal Q∝T. The printed p.144 'Do You Know?' box distinguishes ideal- versus real-gas internal energy and cannot justify arbitrary real-gas isothermal ΔU=0. The original question requests defining/explaining Carnot's engine and its efficiency relation; an authentic derivation and labelled curve should be explained carefully, but no copied publisher figure or unapproved answer edition may be published. The secondary printed outcome P-11-C-23 is Knowledge while this derived calculation and step explanation can be Application-level.
